'''''Anemonoides nemorosa''''' (syn. ''Anemone nemorosa''), the '''wood anemone''', also historically known as '''windflower''' because of [[William Turner (naturalist)|William Turner's]] interpretation of its Latin name ''anemone'' in his 1551 ''New Herball'',<ref name="Turner">{{cite web |title=A new herball, wherin are conteyned the names... 1551 : Turner, William : Free Download, Borrow, and Streaming : Internet Archive |website=Internet Archive |date=2016-10-23 |url=https://archive.org/details/bim_early-english-books-1475-1640_a-new-herball-wherin-ar_turner-william_1551/page/n39/mode/2up |access-date=2026-06-11}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=[[Oxford English Dictionary]] |publisher=Oxford |page=Wh. 160}}</ref> is an early spring [[flowering plant]] in the [[buttercup]] family [[Ranunculaceae]], native to [[Europe]].{{r|powo}} It is a [[perennial]] [[herbaceous]] plant growing {{cvt|5|-|15|cm|in|0}} tall.

==Description==
[[File:Bosanemoon (Anemone nemorosa) (d.j.b.).jpg|alt=Six-petaled white flower|thumb|Typical flower]]
''Anemonoides nemorosa'' is a [[rhizomatous]] [[herbaceous perennial]] plant less than {{convert|30|cm|in|0}} in height. The compound basal leaves are palmate or ternate (divided into three lobes).<ref name="Stace">{{cite book |last=Stace |first=C. A. |author-link=Stace, C. A. |year=2010 |title=New Flora of the British Isles |edition=Third |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, U.K. |page=88 |isbn=978-0-521-70772-5}}</ref>{{rp|106}} They grow from underground root-like stems called [[rhizome]]s and die back down by mid summer (summer dormant).

The plants flower in spring, typically from March to May in the [[British Isles]]<ref name="CTW">{{cite book |vauthors=Clapham AR, Tutin TG, Warburg EF |date=1981 |title=Excursion Flora of the British Isles |edition=3 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0-521-23290-2 }}</ref>{{rp|28}} soon after the foliage emerges from the ground. The [[flower]]s are solitary, held above the foliage on short stems, with a whorl of three palmate or palmately-lobed leaflike bracts beneath. The flowers are {{convert|2|cm|in|1}} diameter, with six or seven (rarely up to 12) [[tepal]]s (petal-like segments) with many [[stamen]]s. In the wild the flowers are usually white but may be pinkish, lilac or blue, and often have a darker tint on the backs of the tepals.<ref name="Blamey">{{cite book |last1=Blamey |first1=Marjorie |last2=Grey-Wilson |first2=Christopher |title=The Illustrated Flora of Britain and Northern Europe |publisher=Hodder & Stoughton |publication-place=London |date=1989 |isbn=0-340-40170-2 |pages=110–111}}</ref>

===Similar species===
The [[Anemonoides ranunculoides|yellow wood anemone]] (''Anemonoides ranunculoides'') is slightly smaller, with yellow flowers and usually without basal leaves.<ref name="Stace" />

Wood sorrel ''[[Oxalis acetosella]]'', which grows in similar shaded places, can be readily distinguished by its 3-parted, clover-like leaves and smaller flowers with five white petals and five sepals.<ref name="CTW" /><ref name="parnell">Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora''. Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Raasepori.vaakuna.svg|thumb|upright|Eight ''A. nemorosa'' in the coat of arms of [[Raseborg]]]]
The native range of ''Anemonoides nemorosa'' extends across [[Europe]] to western [[Asia]], reaching as far south as the [[Caucasus Mountains]] in [[Turkey]]. It has been introduced into [[New Zealand]] and elsewhere.{{r|powo}}

''A. nemorosa'' is typically found in shady woods.<ref name=parnell/> The species is common in the [[British Isles]];<ref name="CTW" /> it often spreads slowly, so is sometimes used as an indicator for [[ancient woodland]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.plantlife.org.uk/uk/discover-wild-plants-nature/plant-fungi-species/wood-anemone |title=Plantlife - Wood Anemone |access-date=2018-10-17 |archive-date=2021-03-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308081858/https://www.plantlife.org.uk/uk/discover-wild-plants-nature/plant-fungi-species/wood-anemone |url-status=dead }}</ref> though populations may also develop from deliberate human introduction in new woodland such as reclaimed land and parks.<ref name="Common">{{cite book |last1=Common |first1=James |title=Urban Flora of Newcastle and North Tyneside |date=2026 |publisher=Natural History Society of Northumbria |location=Newcastle upon Tyne |isbn=978-1-0369-7012-3 |page=96}}</ref>

There are [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] populations in [[North America]] at some sites in [[Newfoundland]], [[Quebec]], and [[Massachusetts]].{{r|FNA}}{{r|BONAP}}

==Ecology==
[[File:Apis mellifera - Anemone nemorosa - Keila2.jpg|thumb|Pollination]]

The flowers are [[pollination|pollinated]] by insects, especially [[hoverfly|hoverflies]].<ref name="blank">Blank, S. and M. Wulf. {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120712205805/http://homepage-zalf.ext.zalf.de/programs/show_fp1/detail.aspx?fid=1128&idx=1&idz=2&lang=eng&text=Investigations|title=on seed production and pollinator biology of ''Anemone nemorosa'' (''Buschwindröschen'').}} [[Leibniz-Centre for Agricultural Landscape Research]] (ZALF). 2008.</ref> The seeds are [[achene]]s.<ref name=Stace/>

==In cultivation==
Many [[cultivar]]s have been selected for garden use. The ''RHS Plant Finder 2008–2009'' lists 70 cultivars sold by nurseries in the UK. Some of the most widely available are:
[[File:Symrer1.jpg|thumb|right|''Anemonoides'' × ''lipsiensis'', center, with its parents, ''A. nemorosa'', left, and ''[[Anemonoides ranunculoides|A. ranunculoides]]'', right]]
* 'Alba Plena' – double white
* 'Allenii'{{smallcaps|agm}}<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/26686/Anemone-nemorosa-Allenii/Details |title=''Anemone nemorosa'' 'Allenii' |publisher=RHS |access-date=12 April 2020}}</ref> – large lavender-blue flowers, often with seven petals (named after [[James Allen (nurseryman)|James Allen]], nurseryman)
* 'Bowles' Purple' – purple flowers (named after [[Edward Augustus Bowles|E.A. Bowles]], plantsman and garden writer)
* 'Bracteata Pleniflora' – double, white flowers, with green streaks and a frilly ruff of [[bracts]]
* 'Robinsoniana'{{smallcaps|agm}}<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/92481/Anemone-nemorosa-Robinsoniana/Details |title=''Anemone nemorosa'' 'Robinsoniana' |publisher=RHS |access-date=12 April 2020}}</ref> – pale lavender-blue flowers (named after [[William Robinson (gardener)|William Robinson]], plantsman and garden writer)
* 'Royal Blue' – deep blue flowers with purple backs
* 'Vestal'{{smallcaps|agm}}<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/94034/Anemone-nemorosa-Vestal-(d)/Details |title=''Anemone nemorosa'' 'Vestal' |publisher=RHS |access-date=12 April 2020}}</ref> – white, anemone-centred flowers
* 'Virescens'{{smallcaps|agm}}<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/96660/Anemone-nemorosa-Virescens/Details |title=''Anemone nemorosa'' 'Virescens' |publisher=RHS |access-date=12 April 2020}}</ref> – flowers mutated into small conical clusters of leaves

Those marked {{smallcaps|agm}} are recipients of the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]. 

''Anemonoides'' × ''lipsiensis'', a hybrid between ''A. nemorosa'' and ''A. ranunculoides'',{{r|astuti2019}} has pale yellow flowers; ''A. ''× ''lipsiensis'' 'Pallida' is the best-known result of this cross. It has also been awarded the AGM.{{r|agmpallida}}<!-- NB for editors: Please keep hybrid × signs outside inverted commas, otherwise they will appear italicised on certain browsers -->
